activities.anchor: Nothing about the robot has changed
activities.caption: pair each question with its C-space rewrite
activities.name: cfgMoveMatch

config.prompt: The abstraction's translations — pair each question with its rewrite:

pairs.right: one point drifting through a six-dimensional space

pairs.left: 'Can the arm reach around the pillar without hitting it?'
pairs.right: Can a path between two points avoid certain forbidden regions?

config.why: Nothing physical has changed — everything about the problems has. And because every robot has a configuration, one set of tools serves grippers, wheels, snake spines and humanoids alike.

activities.anchor: the number of independent numbers needed to pin down
activities.caption: fill the counting rules
activities.name: cfgCountCloze

config.text: A free rigid body in the plane needs %%0%% numbers — two positions, one rotation; in space it needs %%1%%. A revolute joint contributes %%2%% freedom; a ball-and-socket joint contributes %%3%%.

activities.anchor: no quality of motor rescues you
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the actuator audit
activities.name: cfgGrublerSpot

config.prompt: One line of this design audit is wrong — click it:
lines: Grübler's formula is honest bookkeeping for linkages whose joints form loops that constrain each other.
The four-bar sits inside your windshield wiper and a thousand engines.
With fewer degrees of freedom than actuators, a mechanism flops uncontrolled; with more, it binds and fights itself.
A correct count is the design's certificate: the linkage moves predictably, never flops and never jams.
One input — spin the crank — determines the whole four-bar's motion.
config.correction: It's the reverse: fewer degrees of freedom than actuators binds and fights itself; more, and it flops uncontrolled.
config.why: Get the count wrong in either direction and no quality of motor rescues you — which is why the formula delivers its verdict from a parts list, before anything is built.

activities.caption: six joints or seven? file the reasons
activities.name: cfgJointsSort

config.prompt: Why 6 and why 7 — file each reason:

items.label: a free body in space needs 6 DOF — place the gripper anywhere, any orientation
slack to reach around obstacles while holding the gripper pose fixed
elephant trunks and human arms — redundancy of the same kind
a 6-dimensional task surface carved inside a 7-dimensional space
self-motion: infinitely many points projecting onto each point of the surface

config.why: That infinity of configurations per pose is redundancy, and it is a feature — not a joint wasted.

activities.caption: drag between workspace and task space
activities.name: cfgSpacesCompare

config.prompt: Two of the three spaces, side by side — drag the divider:

before.label: Workspace
before.text: The set of points the end-effector can physically reach — a property of the arm's geometry, at most six dimensions, usually fewer.

after.label: Task space
after.text: Whatever the job actually lives in — two dimensions for drawing on paper, six for spray-painting a car body, five or fewer for most assembly once fixtures handle alignment.

config.why: The third is configuration space — the joint values themselves. Planning happens in the biggest one: a humble tabletop wipe may demand navigating a 6-dimensional C-space while the hand traces a flat 2-dimensional path. The task never sees the difficulty; the configuration space carries it.

activities.anchor: With links of one metre each
activities.caption: place the annulus's outer edge
activities.name: cfgAnnulusPlace

config.prompt: A two-link planar arm, links of one metre each. Where does the reachable set's outer radius sit?
config.why: Fully extended: 1 + 1 = 2 m. And the inner radius is 0 — the arm can fold the gripper all the way back to the shoulder — so the reachable set is not a disk but an annulus from 0 to 2 m. Most reachable points correspond to two configurations (elbow up, elbow down), which is why inverse kinematics is not one-to-one.

config.prompt: From geometry nightmare to GPS-style map — order the move:
items: The naive check: does a shaped, articulated robot intersect a shaped world, joint by joint — redone for every instant of every candidate path
Compute, once, the set of configurations in which the robot would collide with anything
Mark that whole set as forbidden terrain — the sofa becomes a curved region in joint-angle space
The question 'can the arm reach the shelf?' becomes 'can a path dodge that region?'
Exact computation is hard in high dimensions — so planners sample and test points instead of mapping the terrain in full
config.why: The same question a GPS answers, in stranger coordinates — and sampling is one more reason, not a compromise anyone celebrates.

config.prompt: Discretise every joint at a modest 63 values (0.1-radian steps). How many cells does the grid of a 2-DOF space have?
config.why: 63 × 63 = 3,969 — trivial. Six DOF is about 6.25 × 10¹⁰, dead on arrival; a humanoid's 30-plus DOF is physically absurd to store. Hence the sampling-based planners — RRT and probabilistic roadmaps — which never enumerate, trading guaranteed optimality for probabilistic completeness.
config.context: Grids die of dimensionality; samplers probe instead.
